modules.title: Pediatric assessment, comfort and medication safety
Infant growth, development and health promotion
Toddler and preschool growth and health promotion
School-age and adolescent growth and health promotion

topics.title: Medication administration and techniques
topics.recognize: Immature kidneys and liver change drug handling; the correct adult dose cannot simply be scaled down.
topics.act: Check allergies, weight in kilograms, safe dose, route and measuring device. Give oral medicines in a small approved volume, never a full bottle.
topics.remember: Offer a choice of how, not whether; never call medicine candy. Reassess effect and adverse reactions.

topics.title: Therapeutic communication
topics.recognize: Developmental ability determines how a child understands illness, time and instructions; caregiver anxiety also affects the child.
topics.act: Use short, honest explanations, medical play and limited real choices. Speak directly to the child and include the caregiver.
topics.remember: Demonstrate unfamiliar procedures; never promise that a painful procedure will not hurt. Adolescents need privacy and participation.

topics.title: Diagnostic procedures and specimen collection
topics.recognize: Fear and movement can interfere with testing; contaminated specimens can produce misleading results.
topics.act: Explain at the child's level, use comfort positioning and collect the correct specimen with ordered technique. Label promptly and check preparation requirements.
topics.remember: Use least invasive steps first when appropriate. A urine collection bag carries contamination risk; a positive bag result needs proper confirmation.
topics.mnemonic: A specimen jar has a clean gate: keep outside germs out so the result reflects the child.

topics.title: Hospitalization and perception of illness
topics.recognize: Separation, unfamiliar routines and loss of control may cause crying, withdrawal or regression; reaction varies with developmental stage.
topics.act: Encourage caregiver presence, familiar comfort objects and home routines. Preserve age-appropriate independence and therapeutic play.
topics.remember: A quiet, withdrawn child may still be distressed. Toddlers need routines; school-age children need competence; adolescents need privacy and peer contact.

topics.title: Pain assessment and management
topics.recognize: Use self-report when the child can reliably communicate; otherwise use a validated behavioral scale such as FLACC.
topics.act: Combine prescribed analgesia with comfort positioning, distraction and caregiver support. Reassess with the same pain tool after intervention.
topics.remember: FLACC scores face, legs, activity, cry and consolability. Lack of crying does not prove comfort; monitor sedation and breathing with opioids.

topics.title: Weight-based dosage calculations
topics.recognize: A calculation may be mathematically correct yet unsafe if pounds, kilograms, daily dose and dose frequency are confused.
topics.act: Convert weight to kilograms; find the safe range, compare the order and calculate the volume from concentration. Clarify an unsafe order before giving it.
topics.remember: mg/kg/day is divided across scheduled doses; mg/kg/dose is per administration. Check units, maximum dose and decimal placement.

topics.title: Infant assessment: expected and unexpected findings
topics.recognize: Observe breathing, color, interaction, feeding and hydration before disturbing the infant; compare findings with age-specific expectations.
topics.act: Keep the caregiver close, use a warm environment, and auscultate while quiet. Trend weight, length and head circumference rather than judging one measurement.
topics.remember: Poor feeding, lethargy, respiratory distress or abnormal growth needs assessment; a newborn may show subtle illness signs.
topics.mnemonic: A growth ruler stands beside a calm baby: observe first, then compare measurements over time.

topics.title: Infant development: Erikson and Piaget
topics.recognize: Erikson: trust versus mistrust. Piaget: sensorimotor learning through movement and the senses; object permanence develops during infancy.
topics.act: Respond consistently to hunger and comfort cues. Provide safe sensory exploration, caregiver presence and simple play such as peekaboo.
topics.remember: Consistent care builds trust; separation or stranger anxiety reflects development. Match teaching to what the infant can experience, not verbal reasoning.

topics.title: Infant milestones and growth
topics.recognize: Growth is rapid; birth weight generally doubles around 4–6 months and triples by one year. Motor control develops from head downward.
topics.act: Trend growth and motor, language and social progress. Ask caregivers about new skills and any lost skills; arrange follow-up for concerning delays.
topics.remember: Milestones are ranges, not a race. Loss of an acquired skill is a warning sign, not normal variation.
topics.mnemonic: A baby climbs a milestone staircase; a missing or backward step prompts developmental follow-up.

topics.title: Infant health promotion
topics.recognize: Well-child care tracks growth, development, feeding, hearing, vision and caregiver coping before a problem becomes obvious.
topics.act: Support feeding and oral care, review newborn-screen follow-up and immunizations, and teach a safe soothing plan. Reinforce supervised awake tummy time.
topics.remember: Routine visits include prevention and screening even when the infant looks well. Place an overwhelmed caregiver's infant safely down and seek support.
topics.mnemonic: A well-child checklist surrounds a growing baby: feeding, screening, development and caregiver support all count.

topics.title: Common infant health concerns
topics.recognize: Spitting up, crying and sleep changes may be common; poor growth, dehydration, lethargy or illness with fever needs assessment.
topics.act: Assess intake, wet diapers, growth and overall appearance. Teach urgent evaluation for fever in an infant under three months or for breathing difficulty.
topics.remember: A common symptom is reassuring only when feeding, growth and examination fit. Never dismiss persistent vomiting or an unusually sleepy infant.
topics.mnemonic: A crying baby's alarm has four lights: feeding, wet diapers, growth and alertness distinguish common fussiness from illness.

topics.title: Infant immunizations
topics.recognize: Infants need a series of vaccines, not a single protective visit; missed doses require a catch-up plan.
topics.act: Review the current schedule and record, screen for true contraindications, provide the Vaccine Information Statement and use the appropriate injection site and comfort measures.
topics.remember: Document administration and teach expected reactions versus emergency allergy signs. Mild illness alone usually does not require postponing vaccines; check individual guidance.
topics.mnemonic: A shield grows one panel at each vaccine visit: review the record and finish the prescribed series.

additional_sources.label: CDC: Vaccines when a child is sick
additional_sources.supports: Mild illness alone is not a reason to delay routine vaccination.

topics.title: Infant abuse and neglect recognition
topics.recognize: Injury inconsistent with developmental ability, unexplained bruising, poor care or changing histories raises concern; abusive head trauma may present with neurologic change.
topics.act: Ensure immediate safety, assess injury, document objective findings and report suspected maltreatment through the required process. Support caregivers without accusation.
topics.remember: An infant cannot explain what happened. Teach never to shake a baby and use safe breaks when crying becomes overwhelming.
topics.mnemonic: A protective shield surrounds a nonverbal baby: unexplained injury prompts safety, careful documentation and reporting.

topics.title: Infant safety
topics.recognize: A mobile infant can choke, fall or reach hazards before a caregiver expects it; sleep environments add preventable risk.
topics.act: For every sleep use supine positioning on a firm, flat, clear surface. Teach rear-facing car-seat use within seat limits, close water supervision and removal of choking hazards.
topics.remember: Tummy time is awake and supervised. Safe sleep does not change to prone because an infant has reflux.

additional_sources.label: AAP: Safest sleep for a baby with reflux
additional_sources.supports: Back sleeping on a firm flat surface remains appropriate with reflux.

topics.title: Infant nutrition
topics.recognize: Breast milk or infant formula supplies early nutrition; readiness and growth guide complementary feeding around six months.
topics.act: Support safe preparation and responsive feeding. Introduce age-appropriate iron-rich foods and textures; assess swallowing, intake and growth.
topics.remember: Avoid honey before one year and cow's milk as the main drink before one year. Do not prop bottles or add cereal without a clinical reason.
topics.mnemonic: An infant food gate admits breast milk or formula and safe age-ready foods; honey waits until after the first birthday.

topics.title: Toddler and preschool assessment
topics.recognize: Stranger fear, resistance and short attention span can limit assessment; expected findings differ from adult norms.
topics.act: Let the child stay near the caregiver, demonstrate on a doll, and use least threatening steps first. Offer two acceptable choices and save uncomfortable procedures for last when possible.
topics.remember: Observe play and behavior as assessment data. Approach according to developmental ability, not age alone.
topics.sn: Toddlers - Assessment of Growth and Development

topics.title: Toddler and preschool development: Erikson and Piaget
topics.recognize: Toddlers seek autonomy; preschoolers seek initiative. Preoperational thinking includes egocentrism and magical explanations, so illness may be interpreted as punishment.
topics.act: Give limited real choices, maintain routines and use simple concrete explanations or medical play. Correct the belief that thoughts or misbehavior caused illness.
topics.remember: Parallel play fits toddlers; associative play becomes prominent in preschoolers. Support independence without shaming mistakes.
topics.sn: Basic Chart - Piaget Theory of Cognitive Development I

topics.title: Toddler and preschool milestones and growth
topics.recognize: Walking advances to running, climbing and improved hand skills; language and pretend play expand. Growth slows compared with infancy.
topics.act: Assess gross motor, fine motor, language and social skills across visits. Provide safe practice and investigate loss of skills or persistent developmental concerns.
topics.remember: Toilet training depends on physical and behavioral readiness, not pressure. Praise effort and avoid punishment for accidents.
topics.mnemonic: A child builds a tower of movement, words and play; readiness supports each new skill.

topics.title: Toddler and preschool health promotion
topics.recognize: Routines, play, dental care and caregiver limit-setting shape health during increasing independence.
topics.act: Encourage predictable sleep and meals, active play, oral care and regular well-child checks. Use consistent limits and positive reinforcement; build self-care into routines.
topics.remember: Offer choices within safe boundaries. Preschool medical play can reduce fear; avoid turning health care or medication into a threat.
topics.sn: Preschool - Assessment of Growth and Development

topics.title: Common toddler and preschool concerns
topics.recognize: Tantrums, picky eating and sleep fears often accompany development; pain, poor growth, prolonged distress or developmental regression needs assessment.
topics.act: Use calm consistent routines and assess triggers. Distinguish nightmares, where the child wakes and recalls fear, from sleep terrors with incomplete awakening.
topics.remember: Comfort after nightmares; protect safety during sleep terrors. Avoid assuming every behavior problem is intentional or every food refusal is disease.
topics.mnemonic: Two nighttime doors show a remembered nightmare and an unremembered sleep terror; safety and reassurance depend on which door opens.

topics.title: Toddler and preschool immunizations
topics.recognize: Children may need scheduled boosters or catch-up vaccines; school entry does not replace reviewing the actual record.
topics.act: Check current recommendations, vaccine history and contraindications. Give the Vaccine Information Statement and use developmentally appropriate explanation, caregiver support and distraction.
topics.remember: A severe allergic reaction to a prior dose or component requires evaluation. Keep a clear record and explain expected soreness versus urgent breathing or swelling symptoms.
topics.mnemonic: A school backpack carries a vaccine record and shield: check which protective doses are due.

topics.title: Toddler and preschool abuse and neglect recognition
topics.recognize: Injuries inconsistent with the story, developmental ability or ordinary play patterns raise concern. Children may disclose fear or abuse indirectly.
topics.act: Ensure safety; listen calmly without leading questions, document the child's words and objective findings, and follow required reporting procedures.
topics.remember: Do not promise secrecy or conduct an independent interrogation. Abuse can be physical, sexual or emotional; neglect also threatens health.
topics.mnemonic: A child's speech bubble rests inside a shield: listen without leading, preserve the words and act for safety.

topics.title: Toddler and preschool safety
topics.recognize: Exploration outpaces judgment; poisoning, drowning, burns, falls and choking remain major hazards.
topics.act: Lock medicines and chemicals, supervise around water, use appropriate car restraints and helmets, and provide food sized for safe chewing.
topics.remember: A child-resistant cap is not childproof. Never store chemicals in drink containers; supervision and environmental controls work together.
topics.mnemonic: A locked cabinet, water barrier and helmet shield a curious explorer: changing the environment prevents injury.

topics.title: Toddler and preschool nutrition
topics.recognize: Slower growth can reduce appetite; excessive milk and grazing may displace iron-rich balanced meals.
topics.act: Offer small portions, regular meals and snacks, varied textures and nutritious choices. Assess growth over time rather than forcing a clean plate.
topics.remember: Caregivers choose what and when; the child regulates how much. Avoid choking hazards and pressure-based feeding; evaluate poor growth or suspected deficiency.
topics.mnemonic: A small plate balances food groups while a large milk bottle crowds them out: variety and iron-rich food matter.

topics.title: School-age and adolescent assessment
topics.recognize: School-age children can describe symptoms concretely; adolescents may withhold sensitive concerns when privacy is absent.
topics.act: Explain the examination, protect modesty and assess growth, puberty, function and psychosocial health. Include confidential adolescent discussion within legal and safety limits.
topics.remember: Ask directly about mood, safety, substances and sexual health without judgment. Chronological age alone does not determine understanding.
topics.sn: School Aged - Assessment of Growth and Development
topics.mnemonic: A privacy curtain opens to a growth ruler and conversation: respectful assessment covers body, development and psychosocial health.

topics.title: School-age and adolescent development: Erikson and Piaget
topics.recognize: School-age: industry versus inferiority and concrete operations. Adolescence: identity versus role confusion and emerging abstract reasoning.
topics.act: Give school-age children achievable tasks and concrete explanations. Include adolescents in decisions, respect privacy and acknowledge peer relationships.
topics.remember: Competence motivates school-age children; identity motivates adolescents. Abstract ability develops gradually, so confirm understanding instead of assuming it.
topics.sn: Basic Chart - Piaget Theory of Cognitive Development I

topics.title: School-age and adolescent milestones and growth
topics.recognize: Steady school-age growth changes to a pubertal growth spurt; timing and body changes vary between individuals.
topics.act: Trend height, weight and pubertal progression; assess body image, peer relationships, school function and coping. Investigate abnormal growth patterns or delayed development.
topics.remember: Compare the child with their own trajectory. Avoid treating normal variation in puberty as failure or assuming physical maturity equals emotional maturity.
topics.mnemonic: A growth chart follows one child through puberty: compare the curve over time, not with a classmate.

topics.title: School-age and adolescent health promotion
topics.recognize: Peers, school demands, sleep habits and growing independence influence health choices.
topics.act: Support adequate sleep, physical activity, dental care and age-appropriate screening. Teach substance avoidance, sexual health and safer decision-making; keep school and family supports involved appropriately.
topics.remember: Use collaborative goals and factual explanations. Private, respectful conversation makes sensitive disclosure more likely than lectures or threats.
topics.sn: Adolescent - Assessment of Growth and Development
topics.mnemonic: A teen steers a health compass toward sleep, activity and support: collaborative decisions build independence.

topics.title: Common school-age and adolescent concerns
topics.recognize: School stress, body-image concerns, bullying, mood changes and disordered eating can affect functioning and safety.
topics.act: Ask about school, peers, sleep, eating and coping. Evaluate persistent impairment or self-harm concerns promptly and connect the child with appropriate support.
topics.remember: Do not dismiss sustained withdrawal or major functional change as normal adolescence. Assess hearing and vision when school difficulty suggests a sensory problem.
topics.mnemonic: A school bag carries hidden stress alarms: ask about mood, peers, eating and senses when functioning changes.

topics.title: School-age and adolescent immunizations
topics.recognize: Boosters and adolescent vaccines maintain protection; records may be incomplete after school or family transitions.
topics.act: Review the current schedule, prior doses and individual risks. Discuss vaccines with the adolescent and caregiver, obtain appropriate consent and provide the Vaccine Information Statement.
topics.remember: Use the current catch-up plan for missed doses. Explain expected reactions and urgent allergy symptoms, and document every administration.
topics.mnemonic: A vaccine shield travels from school to adolescence: boosters and record review maintain protection.

topics.title: School-age and adolescent abuse and neglect recognition
topics.recognize: Unexplained injuries, fearful behavior, abrupt withdrawal, sexual concerns or inadequate care warrant assessment in context.
topics.act: Provide a safe, private conversation; listen without leading, document objectively, address immediate danger and follow required reporting processes.
topics.remember: Do not promise absolute confidentiality. Explain safety limits respectfully; physical, emotional and sexual abuse and neglect can occur at any age.
topics.mnemonic: A private speech bubble sits behind a safety shield: respectful listening supports disclosure and protection.

topics.title: School-age and adolescent safety
topics.recognize: Increasing independence adds sports, traffic, substance and online risks while judgment is still developing.
topics.act: Teach consistent seat-belt and helmet use, safe sports practices and avoidance of impaired driving. Assess violence, bullying, substance use and access to dangerous items.
topics.remember: Match guidance to actual activities and risk. Involve adolescents in a practical safety plan instead of relying on warnings alone.
topics.sn: Adolescent - Assessment of Growth and Development
topics.mnemonic: A helmet, seat belt and decision stoplight travel with the adolescent: independence needs concrete safety habits.

topics.title: School-age and adolescent nutrition
topics.recognize: Growth and puberty increase nutritional needs; restrictive eating, poor food access or excess low-nutrient intake can disrupt health.
topics.act: Assess growth trajectory, diet, activity and body image without shaming. Encourage balanced meals with adequate iron, calcium and energy for growth.
topics.remember: Weight alone does not define nutritional health. Screen for disordered eating and support achievable family routines rather than extreme diets.
topics.mnemonic: A growing body's fuel tank needs balanced meals: iron, calcium and energy support puberty and activity.

topics.title: Blood transfusions
topics.recognize: Fever, chills, back pain, rash, dyspnea or hypotension during a transfusion may signal a reaction.
topics.act: Stop the transfusion, assess airway and circulation, maintain IV access with saline and new tubing per protocol, and notify the provider/blood bank.
topics.remember: Verify identity and product before starting; monitor closely. Do not restart suspected reaction blood. Hemolysis and allergy are different reaction mechanisms.
topics.mnemonic: A blood bag hits a red stoplight when reaction signs appear: stop blood, assess and notify.

topics.title: Epistaxis
topics.recognize: Nosebleeds often follow irritated nasal mucosa, dry air, trauma or nose picking; recurrent bleeding can reflect a clotting disorder.
topics.act: Sit upright, lean forward and apply continuous pressure to the soft nose as instructed. Assess blood loss and persistent bleeding.
topics.remember: Do not tilt the head back: swallowing blood hides the loss and may cause vomiting. Persistent or severe bleeding needs further evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: A forward-leaning nose meets a pressure clamp: lean forward and squeeze the soft part.

topics.title: Sickle cell anemia and crisis
topics.recognize: Sickled cells obstruct flow and hemolyze: pain, pallor and jaundice occur. Fever, chest symptoms or neurologic changes are urgent.
topics.act: Assess oxygenation and perfusion; provide rapid prescribed analgesia and appropriate hydration. Escalate fever or suspected acute chest syndrome immediately.
topics.remember: Avoid overhydration. Give oxygen for hypoxemia; an uncomplicated pain crisis does not routinely require transfusion. Teach trigger prevention and infection precautions.
topics.mnemonic: Sickle-shaped boats jam a blood river: restore comfort and perfusion; fever or chest alarms need urgent review.

topics.title: Iron deficiency anemia
topics.recognize: Pallor, fatigue, irritability and pica suggest reduced hemoglobin; premature infants and toddlers with excessive milk intake are vulnerable.
topics.act: Assess diet and CBC/iron studies; give prescribed iron and iron-rich foods. Teach safe storage because iron overdose is dangerous.
topics.remember: Milk can displace iron-rich meals. Liquid iron may stain teeth; use the taught technique. Dark stools can occur; adherence and follow-up confirm response.
topics.mnemonic: An empty iron toolbox cannot build hemoglobin: iron-rich food and prescribed iron refill the supply.

topics.title: Hemophilia
topics.recognize: Factor VIII or IX deficiency causes prolonged bleeding and deep joint or muscle bleeding; a painful swollen joint suggests hemarthrosis.
topics.act: Assess bleeding and neurovascular status; give prescribed clotting-factor replacement promptly. Protect injured joints and seek urgent care for head injury or internal bleeding signs.
topics.remember: Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and medicines that worsen bleeding. Do not assume a small external wound excludes serious internal bleeding.
topics.mnemonic: A missing clotting-tool piece leaks into a joint: replace the prescribed factor and protect the joint.

topics.title: Leukemia
topics.recognize: Malignant immature cells crowd normal marrow: anemia causes fatigue, thrombocytopenia causes bruising and neutropenia increases infection risk.
topics.act: Monitor CBC, fever, bleeding, pain and treatment effects. Use infection and bleeding precautions; promptly report fever during neutropenia.
topics.remember: A high total WBC does not mean effective immune protection. Treatment also risks tumor lysis, so monitor ordered electrolytes, urine output and hydration.

topics.title: Nephroblastoma: Wilms tumor
topics.recognize: A painless abdominal mass in a young child may be accompanied by hematuria or hypertension.
topics.act: Avoid palpating or pressing on the abdomen when Wilms tumor is suspected. Monitor BP, urine and abdominal findings; prepare for specialist imaging and treatment.
topics.remember: Protect the tumor from rupture. Care commonly includes surgery and chemotherapy; monitor the remaining kidney and provide family support.
topics.mnemonic: A kidney tumor sits behind a hands-off shield: observe and refer without pressing the abdomen.

topics.title: Brain cancer
topics.recognize: Morning headache, vomiting, gait change, visual disturbance or altered behavior can reflect a tumor and increased intracranial pressure.
topics.act: Trend neurologic status, pupils, vital signs and seizure activity; promptly escalate deterioration. Prepare for imaging and prescribed tumor-directed care.
topics.remember: Tumor location affects the clues. Persistent vomiting plus neurologic change should not be treated as a simple stomach illness.

topics.title: Allergic response
topics.recognize: Anaphylaxis can rapidly cause airway swelling, wheezing, vomiting or poor circulation after exposure; skin findings may be absent.
topics.act: Recognize the emergency, summon help and give prescribed IM epinephrine promptly in the anterolateral thigh. Support airway, oxygenation and circulation; monitor response.
topics.remember: Antihistamines do not replace epinephrine. Teach avoidance, the emergency plan and correct auto-injector use.

topics.title: HIV
topics.recognize: HIV damages CD4 immune cells; recurrent infection, poor growth and oral problems can occur.
topics.act: Support consistent combination antiretroviral therapy, monitor growth and ordered labs, and promptly assess infection symptoms. Use standard precautions and individualized vaccine guidance.
topics.remember: Treatment is long term and adherence matters. Ordinary social contact does not transmit HIV; avoid isolation or stigma while teaching actual transmission risks.
topics.mnemonic: A weakened immune shield is supported by a daily medicine bridge: consistent ART helps preserve defense.

topics.title: Burns
topics.recognize: Skin injury causes fluid loss, infection risk and pain; facial burns, soot or respiratory change raise airway concern.
topics.act: Stop exposure, assess airway and perfusion, prevent hypothermia and provide prescribed fluids and pain care. Cover appropriately and monitor urine output and circulation.
topics.remember: Never apply ice to a major burn. Healing also needs nutrition, infection surveillance and movement/positioning to prevent contractures.
topics.mnemonic: Fire opens the skin's protective wall: protect airway, circulation, warmth and later movement.

topics.title: Atopic and contact dermatitis
topics.recognize: Atopic dermatitis is recurrent itchy inflammation; contact dermatitis follows an irritant or allergen at the exposed skin.
topics.act: Remove triggers, protect skin, use gentle bathing and prescribed topical therapy. Keep nails short, moisturize as directed and watch for infection from scratching.
topics.remember: Control the itch-scratch cycle. Eczema is not contagious; harsh scrubbing and fragranced products can worsen irritation.
topics.mnemonic: An itchy skin wall has cracks: gentle care and prescribed treatment repair the barrier while triggers stay outside.

topics.title: Acne
topics.recognize: Inflamed pilosebaceous follicles cause comedones and inflammatory lesions; severity can affect adolescent self-image.
topics.act: Use gentle cleansing and prescribed therapy consistently. Discuss adherence, skin irritation and psychosocial impact without blame.
topics.remember: Scrubbing or squeezing is not a cure and can worsen injury. Improvement takes time; review medication-specific precautions rather than stopping treatment after a few days.
topics.mnemonic: A clogged follicle has a gentle-cleaning sign: steady treatment beats squeezing and scrubbing.

topics.title: Pertussis
topics.recognize: Paroxysmal coughing, posttussive vomiting or a whoop suggests pertussis; young infants may have apnea without a typical whoop.
topics.act: Assess breathing and hydration; use droplet precautions and prescribed antibiotics. Escalate apnea or distress and follow guidance for exposed contacts.
topics.remember: Vaccination reduces risk. An infant's apnea can be the key clue; do not wait for the classic sound before seeking care.
topics.mnemonic: A coughing alarm pauses an infant's breathing: apnea can reveal pertussis even without a whoop.

topics.title: Impetigo
topics.recognize: Superficial bacterial lesions rupture and leave honey-colored crusts; scratching spreads infection to nearby skin or contacts.
topics.act: Use gentle cleansing and prescribed topical or oral antibiotics. Encourage hand hygiene, short nails and separate personal items.
topics.remember: Limit scratching and follow school-return guidance. Watch for worsening redness, fever or deeper infection; the honey crust is a recognition clue, not a reason to skip assessment.
topics.mnemonic: Honey-colored crust sits on a hand-transfer chain: clean, treat and interrupt spread.

topics.title: Scarlet fever
topics.recognize: Group A strep can produce fever, sore throat, a sandpaper-like rash and strawberry tongue.
topics.act: Assess hydration, swallowing and illness severity; obtain prescribed testing and administer the full prescribed antibiotic course. Use appropriate infection precautions.
topics.remember: The rash accompanies a streptococcal infection. Completing treatment and follow-up matters; new cardiac or joint symptoms require assessment.
topics.mnemonic: A strawberry rests on sandpaper: strawberry tongue plus a rough rash points to scarlet fever.

topics.title: Pediculosis capitis
topics.recognize: Scalp itching and nits attached to hair suggest head lice; the infestation spreads through close contact and shared items.
topics.act: Use the prescribed or recommended pediculicide correctly, remove nits as directed and assess close contacts. Clean relevant clothing and bedding according to instructions.
topics.remember: Lice are not evidence of poor character or hygiene. Do not use unsafe pesticides or share combs and hats.
topics.mnemonic: A comb lifts tiny anchored eggs from hair: treat correctly and interrupt shared-item spread.

topics.title: Pinworms
topics.recognize: Nighttime perianal itching and disturbed sleep are typical; eggs are spread from hands to mouth.
topics.act: Collect the ordered morning tape test before bathing/toileting. Give prescribed antiparasitic therapy and reinforce handwashing, short nails and laundering of bedding.
topics.remember: Follow instructions about repeat dosing and household treatment. Treating the child without reducing egg spread can allow reinfection.
topics.mnemonic: A moonlit itching alarm meets morning sticky tape: nighttime itch suggests pinworms; the early tape test collects eggs.

topics.title: Mononucleosis: EBV
topics.recognize: Fatigue, fever, sore throat and lymphadenopathy suggest EBV; splenic enlargement creates injury risk.
topics.act: Support hydration and rest, assess severe swallowing or breathing difficulty, and teach activity restrictions until cleared.
topics.remember: Avoid contact sports or abdominal trauma when the spleen may be enlarged. Antibiotics do not treat EBV itself; fatigue can persist beyond the acute illness.
topics.mnemonic: A tired child carries a protected spleen shield: rest and avoid contact injury until cleared.

topics.title: Measles
topics.recognize: Fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis precede a spreading rash; Koplik spots can appear in the mouth.
topics.act: Isolate using airborne precautions, assess hydration and breathing, and notify the appropriate clinical/public-health team. Provide prescribed supportive treatment.
topics.remember: Measles is highly contagious and vaccine preventable. Identify exposure risk promptly; a routine waiting room can expose vulnerable people.
topics.mnemonic: Three C balloons—cough, coryza and conjunctivitis—float through airborne precautions before the rash.

topics.title: Rubella
topics.recognize: A mild fever, rash and lymph-node swelling may occur; fetal harm is the major concern when a pregnant person is infected.
topics.act: Use appropriate precautions and assess exposure history; avoid exposure of pregnant contacts and involve public-health/clinical guidance.
topics.remember: MMR prevents rubella, but live vaccine is not administered during pregnancy. A mild illness in the child can still carry serious pregnancy consequences.
topics.mnemonic: A small rash stands beside a pregnancy shield: mild rubella can seriously harm a developing fetus.

topics.title: Varicella
topics.recognize: Itchy lesions appear in crops, so macules, vesicles and crusts coexist; fever may accompany the rash.
topics.act: Use airborne and contact precautions, protect skin from scratching, support hydration and give prescribed treatment for the child's risk level.
topics.remember: Avoid aspirin in children with viral illness. Keep susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts away; follow isolation guidance until lesions have crusted.
topics.mnemonic: A rash garden grows spots, blisters and crusts at once: mixed stages suggest varicella.

topics.title: Fifth disease
topics.recognize: Parvovirus B19 often causes slapped-cheek redness followed by a lacy rash; joint symptoms may occur.
topics.act: Provide supportive care and assess exposure risks. Promptly involve the provider for a child with hemolytic disease or immune compromise and for pregnant exposed contacts.
topics.remember: Infection can suppress red-cell production. The familiar rash may appear after the most contagious phase, so exposure history matters.
topics.mnemonic: Red cheeks wear a lace scarf beside an empty red-cell factory: fifth disease matters especially with hemolytic illness.

additional_sources.label: CDC: Preventing parvovirus B19
additional_sources.supports: People are generally unlikely to remain contagious after later rash/joint symptoms; immunocompromised patients may remain contagious longer.

topics.title: Conjunctivitis
topics.recognize: Red eyes with irritation and discharge may be viral, bacterial or allergic; symptoms alone do not always establish the cause.
topics.act: Clean drainage gently, use hand hygiene and avoid shared towels. Give prescribed treatment and reassess for worsening symptoms.
topics.remember: Eye pain, photophobia or visual change needs prompt evaluation. Do not automatically use antibiotics for every red eye or reuse another person's eye drops.
topics.mnemonic: A red eye stands behind a clean-towel shield: hygiene limits spread; pain or vision change raises the alarm.

topics.title: Fungal skin infections
topics.recognize: Tinea can produce scaly circular skin lesions or scalp involvement; the location changes the treatment plan.
topics.act: Keep affected skin clean and dry, give prescribed antifungal therapy and avoid sharing combs, hats or towels. Assess contacts or pets when advised.
topics.remember: Scalp infection often needs systemic treatment; topical cream alone may be inadequate. Complete therapy even if the visible rash improves.
topics.mnemonic: A scaly ring sits on skin while a scalp branch needs a different treatment route.

topics.title: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt
topics.recognize: A shunt drains excess CSF; headache, vomiting, irritability, lethargy or a bulging fontanel can suggest malfunction or infection.
topics.act: Trend neurologic status, head growth in infants, temperature and the shunt tract. Escalate new neurologic changes or infection signs promptly.
topics.remember: Do not pump or manipulate the shunt unless specifically ordered. Families need a clear plan for recognizing obstruction and obtaining urgent review.
topics.mnemonic: A brain-fluid drain has a blockage alarm: vomiting or altered alertness can signal failed drainage.

topics.title: Increased intracranial pressure
topics.recognize: Changing level of consciousness, headache, vomiting or pupil changes suggest rising pressure; infants may show a bulging fontanel or increasing head size.
topics.act: Assess airway and neurologic status urgently; keep head/neck aligned and follow positioning and ICP-management orders. Minimize avoidable strain and monitor trends.
topics.remember: Bradycardia with widened pulse pressure and irregular respirations is a late, dangerous pattern. Do not wait for the full triad.

topics.title: Head injury
topics.recognize: Confusion, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, unequal pupils or seizure after trauma may indicate serious brain injury.
topics.act: Maintain airway and spinal precautions when indicated; perform serial neurologic checks and escalate deterioration. Follow concussion return-to-school and activity guidance.
topics.remember: A child who initially appears well can worsen. After concussion, use a gradual supported return; no same-day return to risky sport.

topics.title: Seizures
topics.recognize: Abnormal electrical activity may cause loss of awareness, staring or convulsive movements; prolonged events threaten breathing and safety.
topics.act: Time the seizure, protect the head, clear hazards and position to maintain the airway. Give prescribed rescue treatment and seek emergency help for a prolonged seizure.
topics.remember: Do not restrain or place anything in the mouth. Reassess breathing and neurologic status afterward; document the event and recovery.

topics.title: Bacterial meningitis
topics.recognize: Infants may have poor feeding, irritability or a bulging fontanel; older children may have fever, headache and neck stiffness.
topics.act: Treat as an emergency: assess airway/perfusion, institute appropriate isolation, obtain ordered cultures without delaying antibiotics and perform frequent neurologic checks.
topics.remember: Lumbar puncture requires safety assessment when increased ICP is suspected. Follow-up may include hearing testing; contact prophylaxis depends on the organism.

topics.title: Hydrocephalus
topics.recognize: Excess CSF enlarges ventricles; infants may show rapid head growth, prominent veins, bulging fontanel or downward-looking eyes.
topics.act: Measure and trend head circumference and neurologic findings; assess feeding and signs of raised ICP. Prepare for ordered imaging and CSF-diversion treatment.
topics.remember: Early detection protects brain function. After shunt placement, vomiting, lethargy or recurring pressure signs may indicate obstruction or infection.

topics.title: Myelomeningocele
topics.recognize: An open spinal defect contains neural tissue; motor, bowel and bladder deficits and hydrocephalus may coexist.
topics.act: Protect the sac with the ordered sterile moist nonadherent dressing, position to avoid pressure, prevent contamination and latex exposure, and prepare for repair.
topics.remember: Never leave the sac dry or compressed. Ongoing care monitors mobility, skin, bladder/bowel function and signs of increasing intracranial pressure.
topics.mnemonic: An exposed spinal sac lies inside a moist protective nest: keep pressure, drying and contamination away.

topics.title: Cerebral palsy
topics.recognize: A nonprogressive brain injury affects movement and posture; spasticity, feeding problems, communication difficulties or seizures may coexist.
topics.act: Assess the child's abilities and aspiration risk; support safe feeding, positioning, mobility, communication and therapy goals. Encourage independence and family participation.
topics.remember: The brain injury is nonprogressive, but care needs change with growth. Motor impairment does not automatically imply intellectual disability.
topics.mnemonic: A steady brain injury has growing branches of support: adapt mobility, feeding and communication as the child grows.

topics.title: ADHD
topics.recognize: Persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity interferes with functioning across settings; assess sleep, learning and other possible contributors.
topics.act: Use structured routines, short instructions, positive reinforcement and coordinated home/school support. Monitor prescribed medication effects, appetite, growth and sleep.
topics.remember: Medication is one part of care. Describe behavior without blame and verify that symptoms cause impairment rather than labeling ordinary activity alone.
topics.mnemonic: An attention desk has one instruction at a time and a routine clock: structure reduces overload.

topics.title: Reye syndrome
topics.recognize: Vomiting and acute neurologic deterioration after a viral illness can indicate hepatic dysfunction and cerebral edema; aspirin exposure is a key association.
topics.act: Escalate urgently, monitor airway, glucose and neurologic status, and prepare for intensive supportive care.
topics.remember: Avoid aspirin in children with viral illness unless a specialist directs it for a specific condition. Check combination products rather than relying only on brand names.
topics.mnemonic: A viral-illness cloud blocks an aspirin bottle while brain and liver alarms flash: recognize the Reye association.

topics.title: Bacterial epiglottitis
topics.recognize: Drooling, painful swallowing, tripod posture, stridor and a very ill appearance suggest a threatened upper airway.
topics.act: Keep the child calm and upright, summon emergency airway support, and prepare prescribed oxygen and treatment without provoking distress.
topics.remember: Do not inspect the throat with a tongue blade or force the child supine. Airway management comes before routine testing.

topics.title: Asthma
topics.recognize: Wheeze, cough, prolonged expiration and chest tightness reflect variable obstruction. Exhaustion, confusion or a silent chest with distress is dangerous.
topics.act: Assess air entry, work of breathing and oxygenation; sit upright, give prescribed rescue therapy and reassess. Escalate severe or worsening symptoms.
topics.remember: Rescue bronchodilators relieve bronchospasm; inhaled corticosteroids control inflammation. Teach spacer technique, trigger management and the action plan.

topics.title: Nasopharyngitis: common cold
topics.recognize: Runny or blocked nose, sneezing and cough usually indicate a viral upper respiratory infection; poor feeding can worsen dehydration in infants.
topics.act: Assess breathing, intake and wet diapers. Use saline and gentle nasal suction before feeds, with appropriate fluids and comfort measures.
topics.remember: Antibiotics do not treat the cold virus. Check before using cough/cold products in children; worsening breathing or hydration needs review.

topics.title: Bronchiolitis: RSV
topics.recognize: Cold symptoms progress to fast breathing, wheeze/crackles and feeding difficulty; young infants may present with apnea.
topics.act: Monitor work of breathing, oxygenation, apnea and hydration. Use gentle nasal suction and prescribed oxygen or fluids when indicated; escalate exhaustion or inability to feed.
topics.remember: Care is mainly supportive. Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not routine treatment for typical bronchiolitis.

topics.title: Tonsillitis and tonsillectomy
topics.recognize: Tonsillitis can impair swallowing and intake. After surgery, repeated swallowing, fresh blood or bloody emesis may indicate hemorrhage.
topics.act: Assess airway, bleeding, pain and hydration. Report postoperative fresh bleeding immediately and follow emergency instructions; provide prescribed analgesia and permitted fluids.
topics.remember: Expected throat pain is different from hemorrhage. Diet and activity follow the surgeon's plan; caregivers need clear bleeding return precautions.

topics.title: Laryngotracheobronchitis: croup
topics.recognize: A barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor suggest viral swelling below the vocal cords; stridor at rest indicates greater obstruction.
topics.act: Keep the child calm, assess breathing and oxygenation, and give prescribed corticosteroid; significant obstruction may require nebulized epinephrine and observation afterward.
topics.remember: Croup's barking cough differs from epiglottitis with drooling and toxic appearance. Cyanosis, exhaustion or reduced air entry requires emergency escalation.

topics.title: Viral and bacterial pharyngitis
topics.recognize: Sore throat with cough or runny nose favors a virus; fever and tender neck nodes can occur with group A strep.
topics.act: Assess swallowing, hydration and airway; obtain prescribed strep testing. Provide pain relief and fluids, with antibiotics for confirmed bacterial disease as directed.
topics.remember: Appearance alone cannot reliably confirm strep. Complete prescribed antibiotics; drooling, muffled voice or respiratory difficulty needs urgent evaluation.

topics.title: Pneumonia
topics.recognize: Fever, cough, tachypnea and crackles reflect inflamed alveoli; hypoxemia, severe retractions or exhaustion signals deterioration.
topics.act: Assess respiratory effort, oxygenation and hydration; give prescribed oxygen, fluids and cause-appropriate treatment. Monitor response and increasing oxygen needs.
topics.remember: Antibiotics treat bacterial pneumonia, not every viral respiratory illness. Escalate cyanosis, poor perfusion or altered alertness rather than focusing only on fever.

topics.title: Cystic fibrosis
topics.recognize: CFTR dysfunction causes thick secretions, recurrent respiratory infection, poor growth and greasy stools when pancreatic function is impaired.
topics.act: Support airway clearance, infection treatment and nutrition; assess growth, stools and respiratory status. Give prescribed pancreatic enzymes with meals and snacks.
topics.remember: Do not crush enzyme beads. Calorie/protein support and prescribed fat-soluble vitamins help growth; worsening breathing, hemoptysis or dehydration needs review.

topics.title: Influenza
topics.recognize: Abrupt fever, aches, fatigue and cough suggest influenza; respiratory distress or improvement followed by marked worsening raises concern for complications.
topics.act: Assess breathing, hydration and risk factors; use appropriate respiratory precautions and prescribed supportive or antiviral treatment. Early assessment matters for higher-risk children.
topics.remember: Annual vaccination reduces risk. Avoid aspirin during pediatric viral illness unless specifically directed for another condition; monitor intake and deterioration.

topics.title: COVID-19
topics.recognize: Fever, cough, sore throat, fatigue or GI symptoms may occur; severity ranges from mild illness to respiratory compromise.
topics.act: Assess breathing, oxygenation and hydration; follow current testing and infection-control guidance. Give prescribed treatment based on risk and severity.
topics.remember: Breathing difficulty, chest pain, marked lethargy or dehydration needs urgent care. Persistent fever after infection warrants assessment; follow current prevention guidance.

topics.title: Allergic rhinitis
topics.recognize: Itchy nose or eyes, sneezing and clear drainage usually occur without fever; symptoms can interfere with sleep and feeding.
topics.act: Identify triggers, assess associated asthma symptoms, and use prescribed antihistamine or intranasal therapy. Teach nasal-spray technique and practical allergen reduction.
topics.remember: Allergic inflammation is different from bacterial infection; antibiotics are not the routine answer. Wheeze or breathing difficulty needs separate assessment.

topics.title: Otitis media
topics.recognize: Ear pain, fever or irritability after a respiratory infection suggests middle-ear inflammation; otoscopy establishes the findings.
topics.act: Prioritize pain control and assess feeding, hydration and hearing concerns. Observation versus antibiotics depends on age, severity and clinical evaluation.
topics.remember: Finish antibiotics when prescribed; reduce smoke exposure. Swelling behind the ear or a very ill child needs prompt review for complications.

topics.title: Cardiac catheterization
topics.recognize: Catheter insertion creates bleeding and distal-perfusion risks; baseline pulses and limb findings support comparison after the procedure.
topics.act: Monitor vital signs, insertion site, distal pulses, color, warmth and capillary refill. Keep the limb positioned and activity limited as ordered; report bleeding or a cool pulseless extremity.
topics.remember: Use the prescribed pressure and escalation protocol for bleeding. Assess contrast-related risks, hydration and urine output as ordered.
topics.mnemonic: A catheter entry gate has two gauges: bleeding at the site and blood reaching the toes.

topics.title: Common congenital heart defects: flow patterns
topics.recognize: Defects may increase pulmonary flow, obstruct outflow or mix blood. Tachypnea, feeding fatigue, poor growth, cyanosis and poor perfusion are key clues.
topics.act: Trace where blood goes; assess oxygenation, pulses, feeding endurance and growth. Support the prescribed cardiac and nutrition plan and escalate deterioration.
topics.remember: Left-to-right shunts often cause pulmonary overcirculation; duct-dependent defects may require keeping the ductus open rather than closing it.
topics.mnemonic: A heart roadmap has extra flow, narrowed gates and mixing bridges: identify the route before choosing the priority.

topics.title: Patent ductus arteriosus
topics.recognize: A persistent aorta-to-pulmonary artery connection usually produces left-to-right flow; a machinery-like murmur, feeding fatigue and poor growth may occur.
topics.act: Assess breathing, feeding, weight and perfusion; monitor prescribed closure treatment and fluid balance when closure is appropriate.
topics.remember: A symptomatic PDA may be closed, but a duct-dependent congenital defect may need prostaglandin to keep that same connection open.

topics.title: Atrial septal defect
topics.recognize: An opening between atria usually permits left-to-right flow; the child may be asymptomatic, with a murmur or fixed split second heart sound.
topics.act: Monitor growth, respiratory symptoms and activity tolerance; support echocardiography and cardiology follow-up. Significant defects may require catheter or surgical closure.
topics.remember: A small defect may be observed. Feeling well does not eliminate the need for follow-up; activity guidance is individualized.

topics.title: Ventricular septal defect
topics.recognize: An opening between ventricles commonly increases pulmonary blood flow; larger defects cause tachypnea, sweating with feeds and poor growth.
topics.act: Assess feeding endurance, weight, breathing and fluid balance. Support prescribed heart-failure therapy, nutrition and repair when indicated.
topics.remember: Small defects may close spontaneously; large shunts can cause heart failure. Escalate worsening feeding or breathing even when a murmur is already known.

topics.title: Coarctation of the aorta
topics.recognize: A narrowed aortic segment causes higher arm pressures, weak femoral pulses and cooler legs; critical newborns may develop shock.
topics.act: Compare upper- and lower-limb pulses and pressures; monitor urine, perfusion and feeding. Escalate poor systemic perfusion and prepare prescribed prostaglandin or repair.
topics.remember: The arm-leg difference is the key exam clue. Duct-dependent newborns need urgent support, and long-term BP/cardiology follow-up remains important after repair.

topics.title: Aortic stenosis
topics.recognize: Narrowed left-ventricular outflow increases workload; exertional chest pain or syncope is concerning, and critical infants may have shock.
topics.act: Assess pulses, BP, perfusion and exercise symptoms; promptly report syncope or poor perfusion. Follow individualized activity guidance and prepare for prescribed intervention.
topics.remember: Severity determines observation, catheter treatment or surgery. Critical neonatal disease may require prostaglandin; do not dismiss exertional fainting as ordinary fatigue.

topics.title: Pulmonary stenosis
topics.recognize: Narrowed right-ventricular outflow limits blood reaching the lungs; severe disease can cause cyanosis or exercise intolerance.
topics.act: Assess oxygenation, perfusion and activity tolerance; escalate severe neonatal cyanosis. Monitor prescribed therapy and circulation after intervention.
topics.remember: Balloon valvuloplasty or surgery may relieve obstruction. Critical newborns may need prostaglandin when pulmonary flow depends on the ductus.

topics.title: Tetralogy of Fallot
topics.recognize: PROVe: pulmonary outflow obstruction, right-ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta and VSD. A hypercyanotic spell causes abruptly worsening cyanosis.
topics.act: Calm the child, use knee-chest positioning, summon urgent help and give prescribed oxygen and therapy. Monitor saturation and perfusion.
topics.remember: Knee-chest positioning improves systemic resistance and helps reduce right-to-left shunting. A prolonged or worsening spell is an emergency; definitive treatment is surgical repair.

topics.title: Transposition of the great arteries
topics.recognize: The aorta leaves the right ventricle and pulmonary artery leaves the left, creating parallel circulations and severe neonatal cyanosis.
topics.act: Arrange emergency specialist care, monitor oxygenation/perfusion and prepare prescribed prostaglandin and mixing procedures such as atrial septostomy.
topics.remember: Survival before repair requires blood mixing through a connection between circuits. Arterial-switch surgery corrects the circulation; oxygen alone cannot correct the anatomy.

topics.title: Tricuspid atresia
topics.recognize: The tricuspid opening is absent, preventing direct right-atrium-to-right-ventricle flow; cyanosis depends on mixing and pulmonary blood supply.
topics.act: Monitor oxygenation, perfusion and feeding; escalate worsening cyanosis or lethargy. Give prescribed prostaglandin when flow is duct dependent and watch for apnea/hypotension.
topics.remember: Blood needs an alternate route between chambers. Management often uses staged surgical palliation with long-term congenital-cardiology follow-up.

topics.title: Kawasaki disease
topics.recognize: Persistent fever with red eyes, oral changes, rash, extremity changes or cervical lymphadenopathy suggests vasculitis; incomplete presentations occur.
topics.act: Arrange prompt evaluation, monitor cardiac status and hydration, and support echocardiography plus prescribed IVIG and aspirin under specialist direction.
topics.remember: Coronary artery injury is the major concern. Keep cardiac follow-up and check live-vaccine timing after IVIG; aspirin here is specialist-directed.

topics.title: Rheumatic fever
topics.recognize: An immune response after group A strep can cause migratory joint pain, carditis, chorea, rash or nodules.
topics.act: Assess cardiac symptoms, perfusion and joint pain; support prescribed strep eradication, anti-inflammatory treatment and activity limits.
topics.remember: Diagnosis uses the overall criteria and evidence of preceding infection. Ongoing antibiotic prophylaxis may prevent recurrence and further valve injury; adherence matters after symptoms improve.

topics.title: Cast care
topics.recognize: Swelling, increasing pain, numbness, cool digits or poor capillary refill can indicate compromised circulation or pressure injury.
topics.act: Check neurovascular status regularly, keep the cast dry and protect edges and skin. Report increasing pain or sensory/circulatory changes promptly.
topics.remember: Never place objects inside the cast. A present pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome; escalating pain with passive stretch is a warning.
topics.mnemonic: A cast has a window of toe gauges: color, warmth, movement, feeling and pain reveal trouble.

topics.title: Traction care
topics.recognize: Traction maintains alignment using continuous prescribed pull; disrupted alignment or ineffective weights can impair treatment.
topics.act: Maintain body alignment and countertraction, keep weights hanging freely, and assess skin, pin sites and distal neurovascular status as appropriate.
topics.remember: Do not remove or alter weights without an order. Prevent immobility complications and report infection signs, severe pain or altered sensation/circulation.
topics.mnemonic: A straight bone is balanced by freely hanging weights: traction works only when prescribed alignment and pull remain intact.

topics.title: Scoliosis
topics.recognize: Uneven shoulders or hips and a rib prominence on forward bending suggest a lateral spinal curve with rotation.
topics.act: Assess posture, function and ordered imaging; support prescribed bracing, skin care and body image. Report new neurologic symptoms.
topics.remember: Observation, bracing or surgery depends on curve size and remaining growth. After surgery, follow movement precautions and monitor neurologic status and complications.

topics.title: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
topics.recognize: Hip instability may cause limited abduction, unequal leg lengths or abnormal screening findings; assessment and imaging depend on age.
topics.act: Support prescribed harness/cast treatment and monitor skin, perfusion and movement. Teach caregivers not to adjust harness straps without instructions.
topics.remember: The goal is proper femoral-head positioning in the acetabulum. Use hip-safe swaddling that allows flexion and abduction; follow-up confirms correction.

topics.title: Torticollis
topics.recognize: A persistent head tilt or preference for one direction often reflects tight sternocleidomastoid muscle; head flattening may coexist.
topics.act: Assess neck movement and head shape; support early physical therapy and taught gentle positioning/stretching. Investigate sudden painful tilt with fever, trauma or neurologic change.
topics.remember: Encourage looking both ways and supervised awake tummy time. Do not force stretches or change safe supine sleep positioning.

topics.title: Plagiocephaly
topics.recognize: External pressure can flatten one area of the infant skull while sutures remain open; asymmetry may accompany torticollis.
topics.act: Assess head growth, neck motion and positioning. Encourage supervised awake tummy time and varied head position; arrange evaluation for progressive or atypical shape.
topics.remember: Keep sleep supine on a safe surface. Positional flattening differs from craniosynostosis, where sutures close too early.

topics.title: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
topics.recognize: Dystrophin deficiency causes progressive weakness: frequent falls, enlarged calves and Gowers maneuver, using hands to climb up the legs.
topics.act: Assess mobility, breathing, cardiac function and nutrition. Support stretching, assistive devices and specialist-directed treatment while preserving participation and independence.
topics.remember: Unlike cerebral palsy, muscle weakness progresses. Respiratory and cardiac monitoring remains essential even when mobility is the most visible concern.

topics.title: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease
topics.recognize: Loss of femoral-head blood supply causes bone necrosis/remodeling; a childhood limp, hip or referred knee pain and limited motion are clues.
topics.act: Assess pain, gait and range of motion; follow prescribed activity and weight-bearing limits. Support orthopedic imaging and long-term follow-up.
topics.remember: Treatment aims to preserve hip motion and contain the femoral head during healing. Bracing, casting or surgery depends on age and severity.

topics.title: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
topics.recognize: An adolescent may report hip, groin or knee pain with a limp and reduced hip internal rotation.
topics.act: Stop weight bearing and arrange urgent orthopedic assessment; do not force hip movement. Prepare for prescribed surgical fixation and postoperative restrictions.
topics.remember: The complaint can be knee pain even though the problem is the hip growth plate. Report symptoms in the opposite hip or knee too.

topics.title: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
topics.recognize: Persistent joint inflammation causes swelling, pain, morning stiffness and reduced function; some forms include fever or rash.
topics.act: Assess function, pain and medication effects; balance rest with range-of-motion and low-impact activity. Support prescribed anti-inflammatory or disease-modifying treatment.
topics.remember: Keep ophthalmology screening even without eye symptoms because uveitis can be silent. Fever while immunosuppressed needs clinical advice.

topics.title: Clubfoot: talipes
topics.recognize: The foot turns inward and downward, with an adducted/inverted forefoot and plantar-flexed ankle.
topics.act: Support serial casting and prescribed correction, assess toes and skin, and teach the brace schedule that maintains correction.
topics.remember: Cool or discolored toes, severe pain, swelling or a slipping cast needs prompt review. Early improvement does not remove the need for ongoing bracing.

topics.title: Craniosynostosis
topics.recognize: Premature skull-suture fusion produces an unusual head shape or suture ridge and may affect head growth.
topics.act: Measure growth and assess development, support craniofacial referral, and monitor after prescribed surgery. Escalate vomiting, lethargy or neurologic change.
topics.remember: This differs from positional plagiocephaly, where sutures remain open. Follow individualized wound, activity and helmet instructions; routine repositioning alone may not address fused sutures.

topics.title: Osteomyelitis
topics.recognize: Bone infection can cause localized pain, fever, swelling and refusal to bear weight or use the affected limb.
topics.act: Assess pain, temperature, perfusion and function; obtain ordered cultures/imaging and give prescribed antibiotics promptly. Support the affected area and monitor response.
topics.remember: A child may avoid using the limb rather than name the pain. Complete the treatment course and evaluate persistent symptoms or systemic deterioration.
topics.mnemonic: A bone has an infection alarm beside an antibiotic bridge: fever and refusal to use the limb need evaluation.

topics.title: Compartment syndrome
topics.recognize: Pressure within a closed muscle compartment reduces perfusion: escalating pain, pain with passive stretch and paresthesia are early clues.
topics.act: Escalate immediately for surgical assessment; assess neurovascular status and keep the limb at heart level per emergency plan. Remove external constriction only as directed.
topics.remember: A pulse can remain present. Do not wait for pulselessness; urgent fasciotomy may be needed to prevent permanent muscle and nerve damage.

topics.title: Congenital hypothyroidism
topics.recognize: Low thyroid hormone from birth threatens brain development; newborn screening may detect it before poor feeding, prolonged jaundice, constipation or hypotonia appears.
topics.act: Ensure prompt confirmatory testing and prescribed levothyroxine; monitor growth, development and thyroid labs.
topics.remember: Do not wait for obvious symptoms. Give the exact dose consistently, not in a full bottle, and follow separation instructions for interfering foods or supplements.

topics.title: Hyperthyroidism
topics.recognize: Excess thyroid hormone may cause heat intolerance, tachycardia, tremor, weight loss and behavior or sleep changes.
topics.act: Assess pulse, temperature, weight and treatment response; give prescribed antithyroid therapy and monitor adverse effects. Escalate severe fever, tachycardia or altered mental status.
topics.remember: Beta blockers relieve adrenergic symptoms; they do not correct the underlying immune cause. Medication choice and monitoring require pediatric specialist guidance.

topics.title: Parathyroid disorders
topics.recognize: Low PTH usually lowers calcium and raises phosphate, producing tingling, cramps or tetany; excess PTH tends toward the opposite mineral pattern.
topics.act: Assess calcium, phosphate, ECG and neurologic/airway symptoms. Treat severe symptomatic hypocalcemia urgently with prescribed monitored therapy; follow cause-specific replacement or reduction plans.
topics.remember: Laryngospasm, seizure or dysrhythmia is an emergency. Think PTH controls calcium balance, not blood glucose.
topics.mnemonic: A PTH balance lowers calcium while phosphate rises when PTH falls; a cramping hand signals low calcium.

topics.title: Growth hormone deficiency
topics.recognize: Slowing height velocity with proportionate short stature suggests inadequate growth hormone; a trend is more informative than one height.
topics.act: Track growth and development, support prescribed diagnostic testing and hormone therapy, and monitor treatment effects and adverse symptoms.
topics.remember: The medication product determines schedule and route. Family teaching includes consistent administration and follow-up; unexplained headache or hip/knee pain needs review.

topics.title: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
topics.recognize: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction causes insulin deficiency: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and fatigue; vomiting with ketones suggests DKA.
topics.act: Monitor glucose, ketones when indicated, hydration and insulin delivery. Support the prescribed insulin, meal and activity plan and teach hypoglycemia treatment.
topics.remember: Do not omit basal insulin during illness; follow the sick-day plan. School support, emergency supplies and medical identification help prevent crises.

topics.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis
topics.recognize: Insulin deficiency causes ketosis, acidosis and dehydration: vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath and deep rapid breathing are clues.
topics.act: Follow the pediatric protocol for IV fluids, insulin and electrolytes; monitor glucose, potassium, ECG, perfusion, urine and neurologic status.
topics.remember: Dextrose may be added while insulin clears ketosis. Worsening headache or reduced alertness during treatment needs urgent assessment for cerebral injury.

topics.title: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
topics.recognize: Insulin resistance and progressive beta-cell dysfunction raise glucose; acanthosis nigricans, polyuria or thirst may occur, but some children are asymptomatic.
topics.act: Monitor glucose, A1c, BP and comorbid risks; support family-centered nutrition/activity and prescribed age-appropriate medicines without blame.
topics.remember: Type 2 does not mean insulin is never needed. Vomiting, dehydration, deep breathing or confusion still requires urgent assessment for a hyperglycemic emergency.

topics.title: Phenylketonuria: PKU
topics.recognize: Impaired phenylalanine metabolism allows toxic accumulation; screening identifies risk before visible developmental injury.
topics.act: Ensure prompt specialist follow-up, prescribed controlled-phenylalanine feeding and medical formula. Monitor phenylalanine levels, nutrition, growth and development.
topics.remember: The plan is lifelong and is not a zero-protein diet. Avoid aspartame and follow the metabolic dietitian's instructions to protect brain development while meeting nutritional needs.

topics.title: Galactosemia
topics.recognize: After milk exposure, a metabolic enzyme defect can cause poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, liver dysfunction or sepsis.
topics.act: Escalate an ill newborn, support screening confirmation and promptly provide the prescribed lactose/galactose-free feeding plan. Monitor glucose, liver status, growth and infection.
topics.remember: This differs from simple lactose intolerance and can be life-threatening. Follow the specific formula and food plan; do not eliminate all carbohydrates.

topics.title: Dehydration
topics.recognize: Reduced urine and tears, dry mouth, tachycardia, lethargy or delayed capillary refill suggest fluid deficit; weight change helps quantify loss.
topics.act: Assess perfusion, weight, intake/output and electrolytes; use oral rehydration for suitable mild/moderate cases and prescribed isotonic IV fluids for severe dehydration or shock.
topics.remember: Reassess after replacement. Small frequent oral rehydration amounts help tolerance; poor perfusion or inability to drink needs urgent treatment.

topics.title: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
topics.recognize: Reflux becomes concerning when associated with feeding distress, poor growth or respiratory problems rather than simple thriving-infant spit-up.
topics.act: Assess growth, intake and respiratory symptoms; use the prescribed feeding and positioning plan while awake. Monitor response and escalate bleeding, bilious vomiting or severe illness.
topics.remember: Keep infants supine on a firm, flat surface for sleep. Reflux does not justify prone sleeping or an inclined sleep device.

additional_sources.label: AAP: Safest sleep for a baby with reflux
additional_sources.supports: Back sleeping on a firm flat surface remains appropriate with reflux.

topics.title: Pyloric stenosis
topics.recognize: Thickened pyloric muscle obstructs gastric emptying: progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting, hunger after vomiting and dehydration are characteristic.
topics.act: Assess hydration, weight and electrolytes; keep NPO and correct prescribed fluid/electrolyte deficits before surgery. Prepare for pyloromyotomy.
topics.remember: Stabilize before repair. The classic vomiting is nonbilious; bilious emesis suggests obstruction beyond the stomach and needs urgent evaluation.

topics.title: Celiac disease
topics.recognize: An immune response to gluten damages intestinal villi, causing poor growth, bloating, altered stools or iron deficiency.
topics.act: Assess growth and nutrition, support testing while gluten is still being eaten unless directed otherwise, and provide dietitian-guided treatment after diagnosis.
topics.remember: A lifelong gluten-free diet avoids wheat, barley and rye. Check labels and cross-contact; removing gluten before testing may obscure diagnosis.

topics.title: Appendicitis
topics.recognize: Pain often migrates from the umbilicus to the right lower abdomen with anorexia, nausea or fever; rigidity or diffuse pain suggests perforation.
topics.act: Keep NPO, assess pain and perfusion, and prepare prescribed IV fluids, analgesia, antibiotics and surgical review.
topics.remember: Do not give laxatives, enemas or abdominal heat for suspected appendicitis. Prompt assessment matters because perforation can lead to peritonitis and sepsis.

topics.title: Cleft lip and palate
topics.recognize: Incomplete fusion can impair feeding seal, growth and later hearing or speech; airway or aspiration concerns require assessment.
topics.act: Use the prescribed specialty feeding method, upright feeding and frequent burping. Monitor growth and airway; protect the surgical repair according to the team's instructions.
topics.remember: Feeding and oral-device restrictions differ by repair and surgeon. Follow exact postoperative instructions and maintain hearing, dental and speech follow-up.

topics.title: Gastroenteritis
topics.recognize: Vomiting and diarrhea from infection can rapidly dehydrate children; assess fever, blood in stool, exposure and overall appearance.
topics.act: Monitor hydration, weight, urine and perfusion; use oral rehydration and continue appropriate nutrition when tolerated. Give IV fluids if needed and use infection precautions.
topics.remember: Antimicrobials are for selected causes, not routine diarrhea. Avoid unprescribed antidiarrheals; lethargy, poor perfusion or inability to drink needs urgent care.

topics.title: Intussusception
topics.recognize: One bowel segment telescopes into another: episodic severe pain, knees drawn up, vomiting or lethargy; bloody mucus stool can appear late.
topics.act: Assess perfusion, keep NPO and prepare prescribed IV fluids, ultrasound and reduction. Air/contrast enema may treat suitable cases; complications may require surgery.
topics.remember: Do not wait for currant-jelly stool. Peritonitis, shock or bilious vomiting requires urgent action; report recurrence after apparent improvement.

topics.title: Hirschsprung disease
topics.recognize: Absent intestinal ganglion cells prevent normal movement, producing delayed meconium passage, distention and constipation or obstruction.
topics.act: Assess stooling, abdominal findings, hydration and nutrition; prepare for prescribed diagnostic evaluation and surgery. Watch closely for enterocolitis.
topics.remember: Fever, increasing distention, explosive diarrhea or a very ill appearance needs urgent review. Definitive treatment removes or bypasses the nonfunctioning bowel segment.

topics.title: Constipation
topics.recognize: Hard painful stools and withholding can form a cycle; overflow soiling may occur around retained stool.
topics.act: Assess stool history, diet and red flags. Use prescribed disimpaction/maintenance therapy, age-appropriate fluids/fiber and relaxed toilet routines with foot support.
topics.remember: Do not punish soiling. Bilious vomiting, severe distention or symptoms beginning in the newborn period needs evaluation for an underlying disorder.

topics.title: Meconium plug
topics.recognize: A thick plug obstructs the newborn colon, causing delayed stool passage, distention and possible vomiting.
topics.act: Assess obstruction, hydration and feeding; follow NPO, fluid and neonatal/surgical evaluation orders. A specialist contrast enema may diagnose and relieve the plug.
topics.remember: Persistent or recurrent symptoms require investigation for an underlying disorder. Bilious vomiting or an ill newborn is urgent, even after some stool passes.

topics.title: Meconium ileus
topics.recognize: Thick meconium obstructs the distal ileum, causing failure to stool, distention and bilious vomiting; it is strongly associated with cystic fibrosis.
topics.act: Obtain urgent neonatal evaluation; keep NPO and provide prescribed decompression and fluids. Specialist enema or surgery depends on severity and complications.
topics.remember: Evaluate for cystic fibrosis. Unlike a colonic meconium plug, ileus involves the small bowel; perforation, peritonitis or shock requires emergency treatment.

topics.title: Imperforate anus
topics.recognize: An absent or abnormal anal opening, failure to pass stool or stool from an abnormal site suggests an anorectal malformation.
topics.act: Inspect the perineum, assess abdominal distention and associated abnormalities, and prepare for prescribed neonatal/surgical management. Keep NPO if obstruction is suspected.
topics.remember: Do not force a rectal thermometer or other instrument into an abnormal opening. Repair and bowel-management plans depend on the anatomy.

topics.title: Urine output
topics.recognize: Falling urine output can signal dehydration, poor perfusion, obstruction or renal injury; interpret the trend with clinical status.
topics.act: Measure accurate intake/output, weigh diapers when appropriate and calculate mL/kg/hour. Assess hydration, BP, bladder drainage and ordered renal labs; report abnormal output for age and condition.
topics.remember: A wet diaper count does not replace measured output in an ill child. Watch both low output and excessive dilute urine.
topics.mnemonic: A urine measuring cup sits on a kilogram scale beside a clock: calculate volume per weight per hour.

topics.title: Acute glomerulonephritis
topics.recognize: Postinfectious glomerular inflammation can cause tea/cola urine, periorbital edema, oliguria and hypertension.
topics.act: Track BP, urine, daily weight, fluid balance, renal function and potassium. Give prescribed fluid/sodium restrictions and medicines; assess neurologic or breathing changes urgently.
topics.remember: Think blood and hypertension, versus the heavy protein loss of nephrotic syndrome. Severe headache, seizures or dyspnea may indicate serious fluid/BP complications.

topics.title: Nephrotic syndrome
topics.recognize: A leaky glomerular filter loses large amounts of protein: low albumin, generalized edema, weight gain and frothy urine are clues.
topics.act: Monitor weight, edema, skin, urine protein and intake/output. Give prescribed therapy and watch for infection and thrombosis.
topics.remember: Think heavy protein loss with edema. Families may monitor urine protein at home; report fever, breathing problems or one-sided painful swelling promptly.

topics.title: Enuresis
topics.recognize: Repeated wetting beyond expected developmental control can reflect delayed bladder control, constipation, sleep factors, stress or a medical cause.
topics.act: Assess daytime symptoms, bowel habits, thirst, dysuria and fever. Use supportive voiding routines and prescribed alarm or medication treatment without blame.
topics.remember: New polyuria or dysuria needs evaluation. Follow fluid instructions precisely with desmopressin; punishment does not improve bladder control.

topics.title: Urinary tract infection
topics.recognize: Infants may show fever, poor feeding or vomiting; older children may report dysuria, urgency or frequency.
topics.act: Collect an appropriate urine specimen as ordered, assess hydration and sepsis risk, and give antibiotics guided by culture/severity. Treat pain and encourage appropriate fluids.
topics.remember: Finish prescribed antibiotics; encourage regular voiding and constipation care. Fever with flank pain or a very ill appearance needs prompt assessment.

topics.title: Bladder exstrophy
topics.recognize: Failure of abdominal/bladder closure leaves exposed bladder mucosa on the lower abdomen, often with urine drainage.
topics.act: Protect tissue with the ordered sterile nonadherent covering, prevent contamination and monitor urine, skin and temperature. Prepare for specialist reconstruction.
topics.remember: Do not let exposed tissue dry or become injured. Long-term care includes urinary management, infection prevention, continence support and positive body image.

topics.title: Hypospadias
topics.recognize: The urethral opening is on the underside of the penis; curvature may coexist and urinary flow may be altered.
topics.act: Assess the opening and voiding, arrange specialist evaluation and preserve the foreskin until surgical planning. After repair, protect the site and catheter/stent as directed.
topics.remember: Do not circumcise before evaluation because foreskin may be used for repair. Teach exact postoperative hygiene, activity and drainage instructions.

topics.title: Vesicoureteral reflux
topics.recognize: Urine flows backward from bladder toward the ureters/kidneys; recurrent febrile UTIs may signal the problem and threaten renal scarring.
topics.act: Assess fever and urinary symptoms; support prescribed imaging, urine testing and prompt infection treatment. Encourage regular voiding and constipation care.
topics.remember: Some children need prophylactic antibiotics or surgery, depending on severity. Seek prompt care for fever or UTI symptoms rather than waiting for obvious pain.

topics.title: Hemolytic uremic syndrome
topics.recognize: Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury may follow a diarrheal illness; pallor, bruising and reduced urine are warning signs.
topics.act: Monitor urine, BP, weight, CBC, electrolytes and renal function. Escalate promptly and support prescribed fluid, blood-product or renal-replacement care.
topics.remember: The problem involves blood cells and kidneys, not dehydration alone. Avoid unprescribed antidiarrheals; infection-directed treatment depends on the identified cause and specialist plan.

topics.title: Renal failure
topics.recognize: Reduced filtration causes waste, fluid, potassium and acid accumulation. Acute injury develops suddenly; chronic disease can impair growth, bone/mineral balance and red-cell production.
topics.act: Trend urine, weight, BP, renal labs and ECG when indicated; review nephrotoxic medicines and follow individualized fluid/diet/treatment plans.
topics.remember: Hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema or severe uremic symptoms requires urgent care. Do not automatically increase fluids in an edematous or oliguric child.

primary_checks.label: CDC: Vaccines when a child is sick
primary_checks.supports: Mild illness alone is not a reason to delay routine vaccination.

primary_checks.label: AAP: Safest sleep for a baby with reflux
primary_checks.supports: Back sleeping on a firm flat surface remains appropriate with reflux.

primary_checks.label: CDC: Preventing parvovirus B19
primary_checks.supports: People are generally unlikely to remain contagious after later rash/joint symptoms; immunocompromised patients may remain contagious longer.
